title: The power of nature: The Prelude, Storm on the Island and Exposure
specPoints: Paper 2 Section B: Power and Conflict: The Prelude (extract), Storm on the Island, Exposure

tips.title: Three natures
tips.body: The Prelude: a teacher that humbles. Storm on the Island: an attacker. Exposure: a killer.

tips.title: Personification everywhere
tips.body: The peak strides; the sea spits; the wind knifes; dawn marches. Compare what each personified nature wants.

tips.title: Forms to name
tips.body: Blank verse (The Prelude, Storm on the Island); eight five-line stanzas with a refrain and half-rhyme (Exposure).

tips.title: Interpretations, held lightly
tips.body: Storm on the Island may stand for Northern Ireland; say so as a reading, grounded in strafes, salvo and Stormont.

why.matters: These three poems show nature as stronger than people, and each gives that power a different meaning: a lesson, a threat, a death. Comparing how poets personify nature, and what the personification is for, is a clear way into AO2. They also pair with the war poems, because in two of them the weather is written as war, and a poem about a storm or a winter night can be the second poem for almost any question about conflict.

examples.title: A landscape that humbles
examples.body: People who climb mountains or cross the sea often describe the same feeling Wordsworth did: a sense of their own smallness that stays with them afterwards. The Prelude is one of the first poems to make that feeling its subject.

examples.title: Weather as the enemy
examples.body: In many wars, cold, mud and disease have killed more soldiers than weapons. Owen's Exposure puts that fact into the waiting of one winter night, and asks the question soldiers in every long war have asked while nothing happened: what are we doing here?

steps.title: The Prelude: a boy and a mountain
steps.body:
William Wordsworth worked on *The Prelude* for most of his life; it was published in 1850, the year he died. It is a long autobiographical poem about how nature shaped his mind. This extract, from Book 1, tells how as a boy he took a boat that was not his and rowed out onto a lake at night. The text below is from William Knight's edition; wording can differ slightly between editions, and your anthology may print *cove* where this has *cave*.

>  One summer evening (led by her) I found\
>  A little boat tied to a willow tree\
>  Within a rocky cave, its usual home.\
>  Straight I unloosed her chain, and stepping in\
>  Pushed from the shore. It was an act of stealth\
>  And troubled pleasure, nor without the voice\
>  Of mountain-echoes did my boat move on;\
>  Leaving behind her still, on either side,\
>  Small circles glittering idly in the moon,\
>  Until they melted all into one track\
>  Of sparkling light. But now, like one who rows,\
>  Proud of his skill, to reach a chosen point\
>  With an unswerving line, I fixed my view\
>  Upon the summit of a craggy ridge,\
>  The horizon's utmost boundary; far above\
>  Was nothing but the stars and the grey sky.\
>  She was an elfin pinnace; lustily\
>  I dipped my oars into the silent lake,\
>  And, as I rose upon the stroke, my boat\
>  Went heaving through the water like a swan;\
>  When, from behind that craggy steep till then\
>  The horizon's bound, a huge peak, black and huge,\
>  As if with voluntary power instinct\
>  Upreared its head. I struck and struck again,\
>  And growing still in stature the grim shape\
>  Towered up between me and the stars, and still,\
>  For so it seemed, with purpose of its own\
>  And measured motion like a living thing,\
>  Strode after me. With trembling oars I turned,\
>  And through the silent water stole my way\
>  Back to the covert of the willow tree;\
>  There in her mooring-place I left my bark,--\
>  And through the meadows homeward went, in grave\
>  And serious mood; but after I had seen\
>  That spectacle, for many days, my brain\
>  Worked with a dim and undetermined sense\
>  Of unknown modes of being; o'er my thoughts\
>  There hung a darkness, call it solitude\
>  Or blank desertion. No familiar shapes\
>  Remained, no pleasant images of trees,\
>  Of sea or sky, no colours of green fields;\
>  But huge and mighty forms, that do not live\
>  Like living men, moved slowly through the mind\
>  By day, and were a trouble to my dreams.

**Confidence.** “One summer evening (led by her) I found”: *her* is Nature, leading him. The boat moves beautifully, “Went heaving through the water like a swan”; she is “She was an elfin pinnace”. Yet it is “It was an act of stealth And troubled pleasure”: he knows he is doing wrong.

**The turn.** From behind a ridge, “a huge peak, black and huge” “Upreared its head” and “Strode after me”. He rows back “With trembling oars I turned”.

**After.** “There hung a darkness, call it solitude Or blank desertion”; “huge and mighty forms, that do not live Like living men” moved through his mind and “were a trouble to my dreams”.

steps.title: Storm on the Island: a community against the weather
steps.body:
Seamus Heaney, a Northern Irish poet, published *Storm on the Island* in 1966. It is in copyright, so it is quoted here only in short phrases.

**Confidence first.** The poem opens “We are prepared”: “we build our houses squat”, strong walls and good slate. The collective *we* speaks for a community.

**Nothing to hide behind.** “Nor are there trees which might prove company”. Even the sea, which you might watch “exploding comfortably” from a safe place, turns against them and “spits like a tame cat turned savage”.

**War in the weather.** The wind “dives and strafes invisibly”; “Space is a salvo”; they are “bombarded by the empty air”. The vocabulary is military.

**The ending.** “it is a huge nothing that we fear”: the enemy is air, and fear itself.

**Form.** One stanza of blank verse, with lines running on: no break, no shelter, the storm continuous.

rows: A huge nothing that we fear

check.solution: The weather is described as an air raid: diving, strafing, a salvo, bombardment. Several published readings note the title's echo of Stormont, the Northern Irish parliament, and read the storm as political conflict too. The poem itself names only weather.

steps.title: Exposure: the weather as the enemy
steps.body:
Wilfred Owen served as an officer on the Western Front and was killed on 4 November 1918, a week before the Armistice. *Exposure* was published after his death, in 1920.

>  Our brains ache, in the merciless iced east winds that knife us . . .\
>  Wearied we keep awake because the night is silent . . .\
>  Low drooping flares confuse our memory of the salient . . .\
>  Worried by silence, sentries whisper, curious, nervous,\
>  But nothing happens.
>
>  Watching, we hear the mad gusts tugging on the wire.\
>  Like twitching agonies of men among its brambles.\
>  Northward incessantly, the flickering gunnery rumbles,\
>  Far off, like a dull rumour of some other war.\
>  What are we doing here?
>
>  The poignant misery of dawn begins to grow . . .\
>  We only know war lasts, rain soaks, and clouds sag stormy.\
>  Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army\
>  Attacks once more in ranks on shivering ranks of gray,\
>  But nothing happens.
>
>  Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence.\
>  Less deadly than the air that shudders black with snow,\
>  With sidelong flowing flakes that flock, pause and renew,\
>  We watch them wandering up and down the wind's nonchalance,\
>  But nothing happens.
>
>  Pale flakes with lingering stealth come feeling for our faces--\
>  We cringe in holes, back on forgotten dreams, and stare, snow-dazed,\
>  Deep into grassier ditches. So we drowse, sun-dozed,\
>  Littered with blossoms trickling where the blackbird fusses.\
>  Is it that we are dying?
>
>  Slowly our ghosts drag home: glimpsing the sunk fires glozed\
>  With crusted dark-red jewels; crickets jingle there;\
>  For hours the innocent mice rejoice: the house is theirs;\
>  Shutters and doors all closed: on us the doors are closed--\
>  We turn back to our dying.
>
>  Since we believe not otherwise can kind fires burn;\
>  Nor ever suns smile true on child, or field, or fruit.\
>  For God's invincible spring our love is made afraid;\
>  Therefore, not loath, we lie out here; therefore were born,\
>  For love of God seems dying.
>
>  To-night, His frost will fasten on this mud and us,\
>  Shrivelling many hands and puckering foreheads crisp.\
>  The burying-party, picks and shovels in their shaking grasp,\
>  Pause over half-known faces. All their eyes are ice,\
>  But nothing happens.

**The enemy is the cold.** “the merciless iced east winds that knife us”; “the mad gusts tugging on the wire”. The weather attacks: “Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army”; “Less deadly than the air that shudders black with snow”.

**Waiting.** “But nothing happens.” closes four of the eight stanzas; “What are we doing here?”

**Dying.** “Pale flakes with lingering stealth come feeling for our faces”; “Is it that we are dying?” By the end, “His frost will fasten on this mud and us”, and the burial party find “All their eyes are ice”.

steps.title: Comparing The Prelude and Exposure
steps.body: Two encounters with nature: one teaches, one kills.

visuals.problem: Compare how nature is presented as powerful in The Prelude and Exposure.

steps.title: Methods: personification, sound and form
steps.body:
Nature in all three poems is given a body and a will.

**Personification.** The peak strides; the sea spits like a cat; the wind knifes, dawn marches, frost fastens. The poets make nature an agent with intentions.

**Sound.** Owen uses half-rhyme, words that almost rhyme, so each stanza sounds slightly wrong, like the soldiers' unease. Heaney's short, hard words at the start, squat and slate, sound solid, and then the storm breaks them.

**Form.** *The Prelude* and *Storm on the Island* are both in blank verse, unrhymed ten-syllable lines, and both run on without a stanza break. *Exposure* is in eight five-line stanzas, each ending on a short line.

**Voice.** Wordsworth's *I*, Heaney's *we*, Owen's *we*: one boy remembering; a community; a group of soldiers speaking together.

steps.title: Context: Romantic nature, a divided island, a winter war
steps.body:
**Wordsworth.** A Romantic poet, who believed nature shapes and teaches the mind. “One summer evening (led by her) I found” makes Nature a guide, and the peak her lesson.

**Heaney.** Writing in Northern Ireland in 1966, just before the Troubles, the decades of violence that began in the late 1960s. The weather is only weather on the page, but “bombarded by the empty air” carries more than wind.

**Owen.** Owen first served in the trenches in the bitter winter of early 1917, and wrote from experience. “What are we doing here?” asks the question the war would not answer.

One sentence of context for each poem, tied to a line, inside the comparison.

steps.title: Plan: Storm on the Island and Exposure
steps.body:
Try: *Compare how poets present the power of nature in 'Storm on the Island' and 'Exposure'.*

1. The idea: in both, nature attacks like an army, and the people are helpless.
2. Imagery: Heaney's air raid; Owen's knives and army.
3. Voice: we in both, but a community and a platoon.
4. Form: one unbroken stanza; eight stanzas and a refrain.
5. Endings: a huge nothing that we fear; all their eyes are ice.

Then write the paragraph on endings.

steps.title: Nature as more than nature
steps.body:
A top-level answer asks what nature stands for in each poem.

**The Prelude:** a moral power, correcting a boy's pride and theft; nature as conscience.

**Storm on the Island:** weather, and perhaps political violence; nature as a way to speak about a conflict that cannot be named directly.

**Exposure:** the real enemy in a war where the enemy never comes; nature as the indifference of the world to the men dying in it, and even, in the poem's last stanzas, God's frost.

Offer the reading and hold it lightly: *many readers*, *perhaps*, *the poem allows*. That is the exploration of interpretations the top level names.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on what nature stands for in each poem and how to write the interpretation

check.prompt: Which interpretation of Storm on the Island is explored in the way the top level rewards?
check.solution: The explored reading grounds the interpretation in words and holds it as a possibility. The certain reading overstates it; the literal ones stop before interpretation.

steps.title: The power of nature in one page
steps.body:
Three poems in which nature is stronger than people.

- **The Prelude (Wordsworth, 1850):** a boy, a stolen boat, a peak that strides after him; blank verse; nature as teacher.
- **Storm on the Island (Heaney, 1966):** we are prepared; no trees; the sea spits; strafes, salvo, bombarded; a huge nothing; one stanza of blank verse.
- **Exposure (Owen, published 1920):** winds that knife us; the refrain; the cold as the enemy; all their eyes are ice.
- **Methods:** personification, military imagery, half-rhyme, refrain, blank verse.
- **Pairs:** The Prelude with Exposure; Storm on the Island with Exposure; any of them with Kamikaze's sea.

questions.prompt: Compare how poets present the power of nature in 'The Prelude' and 'Exposure'. Write the opening idea and one integrated paragraph.
questions.solution: In both poems nature is more powerful than the people in it, but Wordsworth's nature humbles a boy while Owen's destroys men. Both poets personify it. In The Prelude, a peak “Upreared its head” and “Strode after me”, a mountain turned into a living thing with a will, and the boy who rowed out proudly returns “With trembling oars I turned”. In Exposure the weather is armed: the winds “the merciless iced east winds that knife us”, and “Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army” attacks the soldiers in their trenches. The difference is in what the power is for. Wordsworth, a Romantic who believed nature teaches the mind, makes the peak a lesson, and the boy is left with “huge and mighty forms, that do not live Like living men” moving through his thoughts: changed, but alive. Owen, writing from the winter trenches of the Western Front, makes nature an enemy that does not teach but kills, until “His frost will fasten on this mud and us” and the burial party find “All their eyes are ice”. Owen's poem is the darker because it withdraws the comfort Wordsworth assumed: nature here has no lesson, only cold.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Heaney presents fear in 'Storm on the Island'.
questions.solution: Heaney builds fear by first building confidence and then removing it. The poem opens “We are prepared”, and the short, solid words of “we build our houses squat” sound as secure as the houses. Then the shelter goes: “Nor are there trees which might prove company”, and the sea, which might look “exploding comfortably” from a distance, “spits like a tame cat turned savage”. The storm arrives as an air raid: the wind “dives and strafes invisibly”, “Space is a salvo”, and the islanders are “bombarded by the empty air”. The one unbroken stanza of blank verse gives no pause, so the attack is continuous. The final phrase, “it is a huge nothing that we fear”, turns the enemy into empty air: what frightens them is invisible, and fear itself. Many readers hear the title's echo of Stormont and read the storm as the political violence of Northern Ireland; the poem allows that reading without stating it, which is how it can speak about a conflict by speaking of weather.

The poem opens “We are prepared”, and the short, solid words of “we build our houses squat” sound as secure as the houses. Then the shelter goes: “Nor are there trees which might prove company”, and the sea, which might look “exploding comfortably” from a distance, “spits like a tame cat turned savage”. The storm arrives as an air raid: the wind “dives and strafes invisibly”, “Space is a salvo”, and the islanders are “bombarded by the empty air”. The one unbroken stanza of blank verse gives no pause, so the attack is continuous. The final phrase, “it is a huge nothing that we fear”, turns the enemy into empty air: what frightens them is invisible, and fear itself. Many readers hear the title's echo of Stormont and read the storm as the political violence of Northern Ireland; the poem allows that reading without stating it, which is how it can speak about a conflict by speaking of weather.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "Exposure is about the weather." What is the better account?
questions.solution: The weather is the method; the subject is men dying of cold and boredom in a war that does not come to them. The student has named the image and stopped.

markScheme.description: The weather becomes the enemy, and the waiting and the cold show war as slow suffering without purpose

options: The student is right: Owen was a poet who wrote mostly about the seasons, and Exposure describes a snowstorm in the countryside of France in detail, with no connection to the war
Exposure is about a battle
The weather becomes the enemy, and the waiting and the cold show war as slow suffering without purpose
Exposure is about a house

questions.prompt: Why does the peak seem to move, when mountains cannot?
questions.solution: As he rows away from the shore the peak rises behind the ridge, and grows as he moves. His guilty conscience reads it as alive and striding after him. The poem shows how the mind makes nature's power.

markScheme.description: Seen from a moving boat, the peak rises into view, and the boy's guilt turns perspective into pursuit

options: Because there was an earthquake in the Lake District that night, which Wordsworth records accurately in the poem, and the mountain really did move towards the lake
Because it is a ship
Because he is dreaming
Seen from a moving boat, the peak rises into view, and the boy's guilt turns perspective into pursuit

examTechnique.body:
**Know what nature is for in each.** Teacher, attacker, killer.

**Compare personification.** The same method, three purposes.

**Name the forms.** Blank verse; one stanza; eight stanzas and a refrain.

**Context in a sentence.** Romantic belief; Northern Ireland in 1966; the Western Front in winter.
examinerErrors: Describing the weather without saying what it stands for.
Stating that Storm on the Island is definitely about the Troubles, rather than offering the reading.
Forgetting that the Prelude extract is about a boy's guilt and awe.
Misquoting Exposure's refrain: But nothing happens.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer compares how each poet personifies nature and what the personification is for, reads form and sound as choices, offers interpretations as readings grounded in words, and ties context to lines.
